The **tbvax** model is a compartmental deterministic model that simulates the dynamics of Mtb transmission and TB disease progression. The model is used to project the health benefits and costs of various TB vaccine strategies.

In essence, **tbvax** is a system of ordinary differential equations that defines the derivatives with respect to time of a set of state variables. The state variables represent a model population which is structured by the following core dimensions:

-   age
-   VXa (vaccination status)
-   RISK (risk status, currently not used)
-   SES (socioeconomic status)
-   HIV stage
-   TB stage

The number of classes in each dimension is specified by the user.\
Mtb transmission is determined by the transmission probability per contact and the number of contacts per day between 5-year age groups specified by contact matrices (see the paper by Prem et al: <https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009098>).\
The R package deSolve (<https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/deSolve/index.html>) is used to move the set of state variables forward in time from the initial state (i.e. the initial conditions).

The most important functions of the tbvax model are in TBVx-derivs-v##.R (with \## currently at 20). The function derivs.deSolve()is called by the deSolve rk() function to move the state variables forward in time. The function derivs.deSolve()uses matrix multiplications to calculate the contributions of different processes (e.g. incidence, progression, treatment, transmission) to the derivatives. The (mostly) constant values in the (sparse) matrices are derived from the XML input file. The R package Matrix is used for matrix multiplications.

The most important advantages of **tbvax** are:

-   *flexibility* (the end user specifies the model in the XML), and

-   *performance* (one simulation run over a time period of 150 year with 82 age classes, 2 SES, 10 HIV states and 12 TB states (i.e. 19680 state variables) takes only 10 to 20 seconds)

In an SIR model defined by (the dot on top of S, I and R indicate the time derivative i.e. dS/dt etc.):

$$
\dot{S}=-\beta \cdot S \cdot \frac{I}{N}
$$ 
$$
\dot{I}=\beta \cdot S \cdot \frac{I}{N} - \gamma \cdot I
$$
$$
\dot{R}= \gamma \cdot I
$$

with

$$
\lambda = \beta \cdot \frac{I}{N}
$$ 

the time derivatives of S, I and R can be calculated by:
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\dot{S} \\
\dot{I} \\
\dot{R} \\
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\lambda & 0 & 0 \\
\lambda & -\gamma &  0\\
0 & \gamma &  0\\
\end{bmatrix} 
\begin{bmatrix}
S \\
I \\
R \\
\end{bmatrix} 
$$


i.e. a multiplication of a matrix and a vector (S, I, R) (that could just as well be a matrix with age groups in columns). This is the basis for all calculations in the TBvax model (though the matrices are larger e.g. 648 rows x 648 columns for parameter matrices and 648 rows by 82 columns for the state variables).
